description:
AstroAnalog is an open-data tool that ranks Earth locations as analogs for Moon and Mars landing and base sites. Using NASA and other open datasets, it scores similarity separately for thermal, hydrological, radiative, topographic and geochemical themes, adds an extremophile habitability layer (temperature, water activity, UV, salinity limits), and validates against known analogs like the Atacama. 

Built with Python, Google Earth Engine, scikit-learn, Flask and Leaflet/Plotly.
summary: AstroAnalog is a screening prototype that ranks Earth locations as analogs for Moon and Mars sites. Instead of a single score, it compares each Earth site with a chosen target on six themes (thermal, hydrological, radiative, topographic, salts and lithology), so users can see where a site matches and where it does not. An astromicrobiology layer then estimates how much of the time a site stays within published limits for microbial growth (temperature and water activity), using three organism-limit profiles, and flags sites that match a target physically but offer little microbial window. Results appear on an interactive map with adjustable theme weights. It addresses the challenge by giving a reproducible, open framework for characterizing terrestrial analogs. The current prototype uses approximate seed values to demonstrate the method; it does not yet produce scientific results.
details:
What it does: AstroAnalog ranks 12 Earth sites against four Moon and Mars targets (Jezero Crater, Gale Crater, Utopia Planitia and the Shackleton crater rim). For each pair it computes similarity separately on thermal, hydrological, radiative, topographic, salt and lithological themes, then combines them with user-adjustable weights. Each site therefore gets a profile rather than one number.

Astromicrobiology layer: using a table of published organism limits (for example the lowest reported temperature and water activity for growth), the tool estimates the share of time a site stays within those limits. Three profiles (growth, metabolic activity, halophile) are selectable, because the choice of limit changes the conclusion. Sites that match a target physically but have a very low microbial window are flagged.

How it works: a Python/Flask app computes similarity from per-site features and serves an interactive Leaflet map with a ranked table. Slope is computed at a common horizontal baseline for all bodies, and absolute elevation is not compared across bodies because their datums differ. Validation is done per theme: each known analog (such as the Atacama, Antarctic Dry Valleys and Haughton Crater) is checked only on the properties it is cited for, and a rainforest site is used as a negative control.

Tools: Python, Flask, Leaflet, OpenStreetMap tiles. Scripts for Google Earth Engine, DEM and lithology extraction are included in the shared project folder.

Current status and limitations: the prototype runs on approximate, literature-based seed values so the method can be demonstrated end to end. The extraction scripts for real data (MODIS land surface temperature, ERA5-Land, Copernicus DEM, MOLA and LOLA DEMs) are written but have not yet been run, so the rankings are a demonstration of the method, not scientific results. Earth cannot reproduce Martian or lunar gravity, pressure or radiation, and the microbial limits come from a small number of organisms and still need verification against the original papers.

Intended impact and next steps: a reproducible, transparent way to screen candidate analog sites with a microbial habitability constraint. Next steps are running the extraction on real data, using monthly time series, and training environment-to-microbiome models with spatial cross-validation, with a write-up planned as a paper.

Creativity: the astromicrobiology constraint and the per-theme profile, which show why a site is or is not a good analog.
